title: Paramount and State AGs Clash Over Trial Date in $111 Billion WBD Merger Fight
excerpt: Paramount wants a November trial while attorneys general and the Writers Guild push for April, as the frozen merger racks up $7 million a day in ticking fees after September 30.
body:
• Paramount and state attorneys general are fighting over the trial timeline in the antitrust suit blocking its $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger, with Paramount pushing for November and plaintiffs demanding April.
  • The temporary restraining order freezing the deal was extended through August 18, with Paramount agreeing not to close the transaction until five days after the trial or June 1, 2027, whichever comes first.
  • Paramount faces a $7 million daily ticking fee starting after September 30 and a $7 billion termination fee if the deal collapses — creating enormous financial pressure to resolve the case quickly.
  • California Governor Gavin Newsom has privately urged attorneys general to settle, warning that blocking the merger could cost the state entertainment jobs.

The Trial Date Battle

Paramount wants a trial to start in November. The 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America want April. In a joint filing on Friday, both sides acknowledged they had failed to agree, leaving the ultimate decision to U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín.

The scheduling dispute is about far more than logistics. After September 30, Paramount will owe Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders approximately $7 million for every day the transaction remains unclosed — a 25-cent-per-share daily ticking fee that translates to roughly $650 million per quarter. If the deal falls apart entirely due to regulatory failure, Paramount owes WBD $7 billion.

Paramount's attorney Jeffrey Kessler has argued that a hearing before September 30 is essential to prevent "very severe harm" to the company. The states, meanwhile, want more time for discovery and preparation, arguing that the merger's sweeping competitive implications demand thorough litigation.

How the Merger Got Here

David Ellison's Paramount launched the $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery earlier this year, pitching it as necessary to compete with streaming giants like Netflix and Amazon. The U.S. Department of Justice approved the deal in June, though its review was clouded by allegations of political favoritism given Paramount's ties to the Trump administration. "This reeks of corruption," Senator Elizabeth Warren said at the time.

Twelve Democratic state attorneys general, led by California's Rob Bonta, filed suit on July 13. They argue the merger would give the combined company control of 27% of the U.S. theatrical distribution market, 30% of anticipated blockbuster films, and 27% of the basic cable bundle — enough to raise prices, reduce content output, and squeeze movie theaters and cable distributors.

"When too few corporations have too much power in markets central to American life, it makes things more expensive, and it makes things worse."

— Rob Bonta, California Attorney General

The WGA filed its own parallel lawsuit the following day, alleging the merged entity would become the largest employer of film and television writers and suppress wages. The guild noted the combined company would account for over 30% of writing jobs in the industry.

Temporary Freeze Extended

Judge Martínez-Olguín granted a temporary restraining order on July 20, finding that plaintiffs demonstrated a likelihood of success on the merits and would suffer irreparable harm without intervention. The TRO was subsequently extended through August 18.

Paramount then agreed not to close the transaction until five days after the trial outcome or June 1, 2027, whichever comes first — a concession that effectively ended the immediate injunction fight but set up the trial scheduling clash. A consumer lawsuit seeking its own injunction was denied after the judge found the plaintiffs failed to show likelihood of success or irreparable harm.

Political Crosscurrents

The case has drawn political intervention from an unexpected direction. The Wall Street Journal reported that California Governor Gavin Newsom has warned people involved in the case that blocking the merger could cost the state entertainment jobs. His office has encouraged Attorney General Bonta to seek an out-of-court settlement.

Bonta has pushed back, saying the states prefer structural remedies — keeping cable channels, streaming services, news outlets, and film studios as separate entities — over behavioral concessions that are "traditionally not proven to be effective." He has also emphasized that a CNN sale alone would not satisfy the states' concerns.

The European Commission approved the merger in July on the condition that Paramount break up its United International Pictures distribution joint venture with Universal. The United Kingdom is still weighing its own intervention. With the trial date yet to be set and hundreds of millions of dollars on the line, the next few weeks will likely determine whether the biggest media deal in recent history moves forward or unravels.
